docs.title: Mathematics of the Islamic World: An Encyclopedic Reference
docs.text:
Between roughly 750 and 1600 CE, scholars working across the Islamic world, from Córdoba to Samarkand, produced one of the most consequential bodies of mathematical work in history. They created algebra as an independent discipline, transmitted and completed the decimal positional number system, transformed trigonometry from a tool of astronomy into a branch of mathematics, developed decimal fractions and high-precision computation, and preserved, corrected, and extended the Greek geometric tradition. When this material reached medieval Europe through translation, it supplied much of the foundation on which Renaissance and early modern mathematics was built.

This reference compiles the contributions of more than fifty of these scholars, organizes their work thematically, traces the transmission of their results into Europe, and follows the threads that connect their discoveries to the mathematics practiced today.

docs.title: How to Use This Site
docs.text:
If you want people: start with the Scholars Master Index, which lists every figure alphabetically with dates and specialties, then follow links into the era chapters where each scholar has a structured entry.

If you want ideas: the Thematic Chapters each follow one branch of mathematics (algebra, trigonometry, arithmetic, geometry, number theory, astronomy, optics) across the whole period.

If you want the story of influence: the Transmission section explains how this mathematics reached Europe, and the Legacy section connects it to modern practice.

If you want orientation: the Timeline gives the whole arc on one page, and the Glossary defines recurring terms.

docs.title: A Note on Names, Dates, and Accuracy
docs.text: Medieval biographical data is often incomplete. Birth and death years given as "c." (circa) reflect genuine scholarly uncertainty, not imprecision in this compilation. Names are given in simplified transliteration, with common Latinized forms (Algorismi, Alhazen, Geber) noted where they matter for the European story. Claims that remain debated among historians of mathematics, such as the exact route by which the Tusi couple reached Copernicus, are flagged as debated rather than stated as settled fact. See About This Project for methodology and sourcing standards.

docs.title: The Short Version
docs.text:
If the entire subject had to be compressed into five sentences:

  1. Al-Khwarizmi's ninth-century Baghdad treatise on al-jabr founded algebra as a discipline and, in Latin translation, gave Europe both the word algebra and the word algorithm.
  2. Scholars from al-Uqlidisi to al-Kashi built decimal arithmetic, including decimal fractions, into the complete computational system the modern world runs on.
  3. Abu al-Wafa, al-Biruni, Nasir al-Din al-Tusi and others turned trigonometry into an independent mathematical science, introducing the tangent function and the law of sines along the way.
  4. Ibn al-Haytham founded mathematical optics and used what is now called mathematical induction-style reasoning and fourth-power summation formulas that anticipate integral calculus techniques.
  5. Through the translation centers of Toledo and Sicily, and through Fibonacci's Liber Abaci, this mathematics entered Europe and became the substrate of the Renaissance mathematics that leads directly to the modern subject.

docs.title: Creator
docs.text:
Creator: Professor Moez Ben‑Azzouz

Professor Ben‑Azzouz brings more than 25 years of experience teaching mathematics at the university level. While he guides students through the details of concepts, theory, and applications, he also enriches every lesson with historical context that grounds abstract ideas in humanity's intellectual heritage. By sharing stories that trace the origins of mathematical ideas, he helps students see the discipline as a living tradition rather than a detached abstraction.

He actively encourages students to investigate the historical roots of the topics they encounter, fostering independent research and deeper engagement. Through this project, Professor Ben‑Azzouz aims to provide a valuable resource for both students and instructors, a comprehensive exploration of a pivotal era of mathematical and scientific flourishing (the Islamic Golden Age) that has often been overlooked in Western narratives but which laid the groundwork for subsequent European and Western advancements.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: An encyclopedic reference on the contributions of Muslim-world scholars to mathematics (with the mathematically inseparable parts of astronomy, optics, and mechanics), their transmission to Europe, and their connections to modern mathematics. Coverage: 69 scholars across eight era chapters, seven thematic chapters, three transmission chapters, legacy and etymology chapters, timeline, and glossary. Audience: students and the general public; the mathematics is shown honestly (with formulas) but nothing beyond early-undergraduate level is assumed.

docs.title: Accuracy Standards
docs.text:
This compilation was drafted against explicit accuracy rules:

  1. Dates. Medieval dates are often uncertain; "c." and "fl." are used deliberately and follow the standard references (DSB, Rosenfeld & Ihsanoglu). Where sources disagree materially, the entry says so or gives the range.
  2. Debated claims are labeled debated. Examples flagged in the text: the spherical law of sines priority (three claimants); the route of the Tusi couple and Ibn al-Shatir's models to Copernicus (mathematical identity is fact, transmission is debated); Sharaf al-Din al-Tusi's "derivative" (Rashed's reading vs. Hogendijk's); the shay → x etymology (plausible, unproven); Ibn Hamza and logarithms (overstated in popular accounts); the almanac etymology (standard but debated).
  3. Sources are real. Every cited book, edition, and article in the Bibliography is a genuine publication. Per-entry source lines point to the standard scholarly literature on that figure.
  4. No invented quotations. Paraphrase is used instead of quotation except where a phrase is a standard, verifiable translation.
  5. Known weak spots are disclosed. The Ibn Hamza entry explicitly notes its thinner evidentiary base. Readers preparing formal coursework or publication should verify details against the census references named in the bibliography.

docs.title: How This Reference Was Compiled
docs.text: Drafted from the standard scholarly literature on the history of Islamic mathematics (Berggren, Katz, Rashed, Van Brummelen, Kennedy, King, Saliba, Sabra, Hogendijk, Djebbar, and the DSB), organized for navigation by person, by topic, and by transmission story. It is a synthesis for students and general readers, not original manuscript research.

docs.title: Suggested Expansion Phases
docs.text:
The architecture supports growth:

  • Phase 2 — Depth. Promote major figures (al-Khwarizmi, Ibn al-Haytham, al-Biruni, Khayyam, al-Tusi, al-Kashi) to individual pages with worked mathematical examples (e.g., Khayyam's circle-parabola construction step by step; al-Kashi's sin 1° iteration executed).
  • Phase 3 — Primary texts. Add a translated-excerpts section keyed to the Katz Sourcebook and published editions.
  • Phase 4 — Visuals. Diagrams (Tusi couple animation, Saccheri quadrilateral, astrolabe projection), maps of centers and translation routes, and a graphical timeline.
  • Phase 5 — Problems. End-of-chapter exercises for classroom use (the material adapts naturally to Calculus II and History of Math courses).

docs.title: Rights and Use
docs.text: Text of this compilation may be used freely for educational purposes. The scholarly works cited remain under their own copyrights; quotations from them have been avoided in favor of paraphrase and citation.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
al-jabr — "Restoration/completion": moving a subtracted quantity to the other side of an equation as an added one. Half of the name of al-Khwarizmi's method; source of the word algebra.

al-muqabala — "Balancing/confrontation": cancelling equal terms from both sides of an equation. The other half of the method's name.

algorism — Medieval Latin term for written computation with Hindu-Arabic numerals, from Algorismi (al-Khwarizmi). Ancestor of algorithm.

astrolabe — Analog computer for astronomical problems, based on stereographic projection of the celestial sphere onto a plane; the standard scientific instrument of the era. The safiha (saphaea) of al-Zarqali is a universal (any-latitude) variant; Sharaf al-Din al-Tusi's linear astrolabe compresses one onto a rod.

dust board (takht) — Erasable computing surface on which Indian-reckoning algorithms were first performed; al-Uqlidisi advertised adapting them to ink and paper.

equant — Ptolemy's device: a point about which a planet's epicycle center moves with uniform angular speed, violating uniform circular motion and provoking the Islamic critical tradition from Ibn al-Haytham to the Maragha school.

girih — The strapwork pattern family of Islamic geometric ornament; connected to the constructional geometry of Abu al-Wafa's artisan handbook and, in modern analysis, to quasi-periodic tilings.

hisab — Practical calculation/arithmetic; hisab al-hind = Indian (decimal positional) reckoning.

ilm al-fara'id — The law/science of inheritance shares; a driver of exact fraction arithmetic and the application field of half of al-Khwarizmi's Algebra.

ilm al-miqat — The science of astronomical timekeeping (prayer times etc.); profession of the muwaqqit.

jayb — Arabic for sine (see Etymology for the mistranslation to sinus).

madrasa — Endowed teaching college; the institutional home of later mathematical instruction (Samarkand's being the most scientifically ambitious).

mal — "Wealth/property": the technical term for the square of the unknown in Arabic algebra (the unknown itself being shay, "thing," or jidhr, "root").

Maragha school — The 13th-century observatory group (Tusi, Urdi, Shirazi, al-Maghribi) and their successors (Ibn al-Shatir) who rebuilt planetary geometry from uniform circular motions.

muwaqqit — Mosque-employed astronomer/timekeeper (Ibn al-Shatir and al-Khalili held the post in Damascus).

qibla — The direction of Mecca; determining it from arbitrary coordinates is a central spherical-trigonometry problem of the tradition.

rub al-mujayyab — The sine quadrant: a quarter-circle instrument with a trigonometric grid, used to solve triangles graphically; an analog trig calculator.

shadow functions — The tangent and cotangent in their original form: shadow lengths of a standard gnomon (vertical or horizontal). Zill = shadow.

shay — "Thing": the unknown, x, of Arabic algebra.

Tusi couple — Two-circle rolling mechanism (radii in ratio 1:2) converting circular motions into straight-line oscillation; introduced by Nasir al-Din al-Tusi (1247/1261 works), used to replace the equant; reappears in Copernicus.

Urdi's lemma — Geometric equivalence (al-Urdi, before 1259) letting an eccentric-with-equant be replaced by concentric circles plus an epicyclet; a second core tool of Maragha planetary theory, also present in Copernicus's models.

zij — Astronomical handbook: theory reduced to tables plus instructions. The tradition's characteristic mathematical-astronomical publication (200+ known); ancestor, through the Toledan and Alfonsine tables, of the modern ephemeris.

docs.title: The Setting
docs.text: The mathematical tradition covered in this reference arose within the Islamic world in the broad geographic sense: the territories from al-Andalus (Islamic Spain) and the Maghreb in the west, through Egypt, Syria, and Iraq, to Persia, Central Asia, and northern India in the east. The scholars who worked in this tradition were predominantly Muslim, but the scientific community also included Christian, Jewish, and Sabian participants (Thabit ibn Qurra, one of the greatest geometers of the ninth century, was a Sabian from Harran; Hunayn ibn Ishaq, the master translator, was a Nestorian Christian). The unifying medium was the Arabic language, which served the role Latin later served in Europe and English serves in science today. Historians therefore sometimes call this tradition "Arabic mathematics" (after the language) and sometimes "Islamic mathematics" (after the civilization); both labels describe the same body of work.

docs.title: The Translation Movement into Arabic (c. 750–950)
docs.text:
The Abbasid caliphate, established in 750 with its capital at Baghdad from 762, sponsored a deliberate, generously funded campaign to translate the scientific heritage of earlier civilizations into Arabic. Three streams mattered most for mathematics:

The Greek stream. Euclid's Elements, Ptolemy's Almagest, the works of Archimedes, Apollonius's Conics, Diophantus's Arithmetica, and Menelaus's Spherics were translated, often multiple times with increasing precision. Translators such as al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf ibn Matar, Hunayn ibn Ishaq, his son Ishaq ibn Hunayn, and Thabit ibn Qurra (who revised many translations) made Baghdad the custodian of Greek mathematics at a time when much of it was inaccessible in Western Europe.

The Indian stream. Sanskrit astronomical works (the siddhanta tradition, rendered in Arabic as Sindhind) arrived at the Abbasid court in the 770s, carrying with them the decimal positional numeral system, the zero, and Indian trigonometry based on the sine rather than the Greek chord.

The Persian stream. Sasanian astronomical tables (zij) and administrative computational practice contributed to the applied side of the tradition.

docs.title: The House of Wisdom
docs.text: The Bayt al-Hikma (House of Wisdom) in Baghdad, associated especially with the caliph al-Ma'mun (r. 813–833), functioned as a library, translation center, and research institution. Its exact institutional nature is debated by historians, and popular accounts sometimes overstate its resemblance to a modern university. What is not debated is the roster of mathematicians connected with al-Ma'mun's patronage: al-Khwarizmi, the three Banu Musa brothers, and al-Kindi all worked in this Baghdad milieu, and the observational astronomy program al-Ma'mun sponsored (including a measurement of the Earth's circumference) set the pattern of state-supported exact science that later courts imitated.

docs.title: Why Mathematics Flourished
docs.text:
Several forces sustained mathematical work across nine centuries:

Religious practice generated computational problems. Determining prayer times requires spherical astronomy; finding the qibla (direction of Mecca) from any city is a genuinely hard problem in spherical trigonometry; the lunar calendar demands visibility calculations; and Islamic inheritance law ('ilm al-fara'id) requires exact fractional arithmetic, which al-Khwarizmi treated at length in his algebra. A specialized professional, the muwaqqit (timekeeper attached to a mosque), emerged; al-Khalili in fourteenth-century Damascus, who computed universal auxiliary tables for spherical astronomy, held such a post.

Commerce and administration demanded arithmetic. The vast trade networks of the Islamic world ran on computation, and treatises on hisab (practical reckoning) were bestsellers of the manuscript era.

Courts competed for prestige. From Baghdad to Cairo (the Fatimid observatory), Rayy, Isfahan (where Omar Khayyam reformed the calendar), Maragha (the great observatory founded in 1259), and Samarkand (Ulugh Beg's observatory and madrasa, c. 1420s), rulers funded observatories and salaried scholars in a pattern that resembles modern national laboratories more than anything in contemporary Europe.

Astronomy and astrology paid the bills. As in Kepler's Europe centuries later, the demand for astronomical tables and astrological services financed a great deal of pure mathematics.

docs.title: Periodization Used in This Reference
docs.text: Era Span Centers Signature achievements I. Foundations 750–900 Baghdad Translation movement; al-Khwarizmi's algebra; Thabit's geometry and number theory II. Tenth century 900–1000 Baghdad, Rayy, Cairo, Córdoba Decimal fractions (al-Uqlidisi); trigonometric functions completed (Abu al-Wafa); geometric constructions III. Golden age c. 1000–1100 Ghazna, Cairo, Isfahan, al-Andalus Ibn al-Haytham's optics; al-Biruni's geodesy; al-Karaji's algebra of polynomials; Khayyam's cubics IV. Twelfth century 1100–1200 Persia, al-Andalus, Maghreb al-Samawal's symbolic methods; Sharaf al-Din al-Tusi's analysis of cubics V. Maragha 1200–1300 Maragha, Maghreb Tusi's trigonometry as independent science; planetary theory (Tusi couple) VI. Fourteenth century 1300–1400 Damascus, Persia, Maghreb Ibn al-Shatir's planetary models; al-Farisi's number theory and optics; al-Khalili's tables VII. Samarkand 1400–1500 Samarkand, Maghreb, Cairo al-Kashi's computational mathematics; Ulugh Beg's star catalog; al-Qalasadi's algebraic notation VIII. Later scholars 1500 onward Istanbul, Persia, Maghreb Taqi al-Din's observatory; continued textbook tradition

docs.title: What Came Before and After
docs.text:
This tradition did not arise from nothing and did not vanish into nothing. It consciously absorbed Greek, Indian, and Persian mathematics, and it was in turn absorbed, through the Latin translation movement of the twelfth century and the commercial mathematics of the Italian abacus schools, into the European tradition that leads to the Renaissance algebraists, to Viète and Descartes, and onward to the modern discipline. The Transmission chapters follow that story in detail.

Primary secondary sources for this chapter: J. L. Berggren, Episodes in the Mathematics of Medieval Islam; Victor J. Katz, A History of Mathematics; George Saliba, Islamic Science and the Making of the European Renaissance; Dimitri Gutas, Greek Thought, Arabic Culture. Full details in the Bibliography.

docs.title: Etymology of Mathematical Terms
docs.text: Ordinary technical vocabulary preserves the transmission history like tree rings. Each entry below gives the standard etymology; where an etymology is folk or disputed, that is said.

docs.title: algebra
docs.text: From al-jabr ("the restoring/completion"), the first operation in the title of al-Khwarizmi's treatise al-Kitab al-mukhtasar fi hisab al-jabr wa-l-muqabala. In medieval Spanish and Italian, an algebrista could also mean a bone-setter, one who restores what is broken, the same Arabic sense applied to fractures. The mathematical meaning won.

docs.title: algorithm / algorism
docs.text: From Algorismi/Algoritmi, the Latinization of al-Khwarizmi's name in the translations of his arithmetic (Dixit Algorizmi). Medieval algorism = computation with Hindu-Arabic numerals; the modern spelling and generalized sense (any effective procedure) were influenced by false association with Greek arithmos (number). A ninth-century Baghdad civil servant's hometown surname (Khwarazm, the region south of the Aral Sea) is now the central noun of computer science.

docs.title: cipher, zero
docs.text: Both from Arabic sifr ("empty"), translating Sanskrit sunya (the empty place in positional notation). Latin cifra/cephirum split into two words: Italian zefiro → zero (the digit), and cipher (first meaning the zero, then any numeral, then secret writing, the last sense probably because encoded text looked like meaningless numerals). One Arabic word, two fundamental modern terms in mathematics and cryptography.

docs.title: sine
docs.text: The famous mistranslation. Sanskrit jya/jiva (bow-string, the half-chord) was transliterated into Arabic as j-y-b; read as the genuine Arabic word jayb (fold, pocket, bosom of a garment), it was translated into Latin as sinus (fold, bay). See Trigonometry. The other function names are Latin add-ons: cosinus (complement's sine), tangens and secans (touching and cutting lines, introduced by Thomas Fincke, 1583), but tangent and cotangent as functions originate as the Islamic shadow functions (zill, shadow).

docs.title: zenith
docs.text: From Arabic samt al-ra's ("direction of the head," the point overhead). In manuscript Latin, samt was miscopied, an m read as ni, yielding senit/cenit → zenith. A scribal error is permanently installed in every astronomy textbook.

docs.title: nadir
docs.text: From nazir ("opposite"), as in nazir al-samt, the point opposite the zenith. Clean transmission, no scribal accident this time.

docs.title: azimuth
docs.text: From al-sumut, plural of the same samt (direction): the compass bearings along the horizon.

docs.title: almanac
docs.text: From Arabic al-manakh, attested in al-Andalus for astronomical calendars/tables; the word's own deeper origin is uncertain (this is the standard but debated etymology, flagged as such in the OED).

docs.title: almagest
docs.text: Ptolemy's Syntaxis became, in the Islamic world, al-majisti (from Greek megiste, "the greatest"), and returned to Europe as Almagest, a Greek superlative wearing an Arabic article, the whole transmission story in a single word.

docs.title: Other survivals
docs.text: Alidade (the sighting rule of an astrolabe, al-idada); alcohol and alkali and alchemy/chemistry from the allied sciences; nucha (anatomy) and a hundred medical terms; and the star names: Aldebaran (al-dabaran, "the follower"), Altair (al-ta'ir, "the flying [eagle]"), Betelgeuse (yad al-jawza, "the hand of Orion," mangled in transliteration), Deneb (dhanab, "tail"), Rigel (rijl, "foot"), Vega (from al-nasr al-waqi, "the swooping eagle"), Fomalhaut (fam al-hut, "the fish's mouth"), Algol (ra's al-ghul, "the demon's head"). Roughly two hundred named stars carry Arabic names, most fixed in European usage through Latin translations of Arabic astronomical tables.

docs.title: And the letter x?
docs.text:
The claim that the algebraic x descends from Arabic shay ("thing," the unknown), via Old Spanish transcription with x (then pronounced "sh"), is attractive and repeated widely; the sober assessment is that direct documentary proof is lacking, and Descartes' typographic conventions in the Géométrie (1637) are the proximate source of x-y-z for unknowns. This reference reports the shay story as plausible but unproven.

Sources: OED etymologies; Katz; Berggren; Kunitzsch, The Arabs and the Stars (star-name scholarship); standard histories of mathematical notation (Cajori).

docs.title: Lines to Modern Mathematics
docs.text:
This chapter collects, in one place, the threads that run from the Islamic tradition into mathematics as practiced now. Threads differ in kind: some are direct lineage (unbroken textual and pedagogical descent), some are documented influence (specific transmission events), and some are anticipations (the tradition got there first, but moderns rebuilt independently). The label matters; the table says which is which.

docs.title: Three Larger Points
docs.text:
1. The "warehouse" myth fails on the evidence. The claim that the Islamic world merely stored Greek learning until Europe wanted it back cannot survive contact with al-Karaji's polynomials, al-Kashi's numerics, Ibn al-Haytham's experiments, al-Khalili's tables, or the fact that the most original material never reached Europe at all and had to be excavated by modern historians (Woepcke, Luckey, Kennedy, Saidan, Rashed, King, Hogendijk, Berggren, Djebbar, and their students). What Europe received was transformative; what it did not receive proves the tradition's originality.

2. Anticipation without transmission still matters. Cases like Ceva's theorem in al-Mu'taman, Snell's law in Ibn Sahl, or decimal fractions in al-Uqlidisi do more than assign priority: they show which mathematical developments are natural, reachable from the shared classical inheritance by more than one route, and they calibrate how we tell the history of "European" mathematics, which re-walked, often unknowingly, roads already mapped.

3. The professional culture is part of the legacy. Salaried researchers at funded observatories; textbook series and commentary chains; tables computed by teams to specified precision with error checking; instruments engineered to push accuracy, this is a recognizable ancestor of organized scientific research, and the tradition ran it for centuries.

Sources: as cited throughout; synthesis follows Berggren, Katz, Rashed, Saliba, Van Brummelen, and King.

docs.title: Era I — Foundations (750–900)
docs.text: The first 150 years of the tradition: the translation of Greek and Indian mathematics into Arabic in Abbasid Baghdad, and the first original masterpieces built on that foundation. Dates for this period are frequently approximate.

docs.title: al-Fazari
docs.text:
Ibrahim al-Fazari and his son Muhammad al-Fazari (8th century, d. c. 796–806) · Baghdad · astronomy, instruments

The Fazaris stand at the threshold of the tradition. When an Indian embassy brought Sanskrit astronomical material to the court of the caliph al-Mansur in the 770s, Muhammad al-Fazari participated in rendering it into Arabic as the Zij al-Sindhind, the channel through which Indian astronomy and, crucially, the decimal positional numeral system entered the Islamic world. He is also traditionally credited as among the first in the Islamic world to construct astrolabes. The biographical record for both father and son is thin and partly conflated in medieval sources; historians flag most personal details as uncertain.

Sources: DSB (D. Pingree, "al-Fazari"); Katz, ch. on Islamic mathematics.

docs.title: al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf ibn Matar
docs.text:
al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf ibn Matar (fl. c. 786–833) · Baghdad · translation

The first known translator of Euclid's Elements into Arabic, producing one version under Harun al-Rashid and a revised version under al-Ma'mun. He also translated Ptolemy's Almagest. His translations made the axiomatic-deductive method of Greek geometry available to the Arabic-reading world, and the Elements he transmitted became the universal geometry textbook of the tradition. Portions of the Latin Euclid that medieval Europe used descend, through later Arabic recensions, from the Hajjaj line of transmission.

Sources: DSB; Berggren, Episodes, ch. 1.

docs.title: Hunayn ibn Ishaq and Ishaq ibn Hunayn
docs.text:
Hunayn ibn Ishaq (809–873) and Ishaq ibn Hunayn (c. 830–910/911) · Baghdad · translation

Hunayn, a Nestorian Christian physician, headed the most productive translation workshop of the ninth century and set new philological standards, collating multiple Greek manuscripts before translating. While his own output centered on medicine, his son Ishaq produced the translations of Euclid's Elements and Ptolemy's Almagest that, as revised by Thabit ibn Qurra, became the standard mathematical texts of the Islamic world. The Ishaq–Thabit Elements is the version most Islamic geometers actually read.

Sources: DSB; Gutas, Greek Thought, Arabic Culture.

docs.title: al-Khwarizmi
docs.text:
Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi (c. 780 – c. 850) · Baghdad (House of Wisdom) · algebra, arithmetic, astronomy, geography

The most influential mathematician of the era and arguably of the entire tradition. Two works define his legacy:

The Algebra. Al-Kitab al-mukhtasar fi hisab al-jabr wa-l-muqabala ("The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing," c. 820s) is the founding document of algebra as an independent discipline. Al-Khwarizmi classified equations of degree at most two into six standard types (in modern notation: \(ax^2 = bx\), \(ax^2 = c\), \(bx = c\), \(ax^2 + bx = c\), \(ax^2 + c = bx\), \(ax^2 = bx + c\), all with positive coefficients), gave systematic solution procedures for each, and supplied geometric justifications in the style of completing the square, literally, with squares. The operations al-jabr (restoring, moving a subtracted term across the equation) and al-muqabala (balancing, cancelling like terms) gave the discipline its name: algebra. The book's second half applies the method to inheritance problems, mensuration, and commerce; it is a manual for solving problems, not a commentary on Greek geometry, and this problem-solving orientation is precisely what was new.

The Arithmetic. His treatise on reckoning with Hindu numerals survives only in Latin versions (the tradition beginning Dixit Algorizmi, "Thus spoke al-Khwarizmi"). It taught place-value notation, the zero, and the algorithms for addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and root extraction. The Latinization of his name, Algorismi, became the medieval word algorism (decimal computation) and ultimately the modern word algorithm.

He also compiled the Zij al-Sindhind astronomical tables (the first major original zij of the tradition, blending Indian, Persian, and Greek methods) and a Book of the Depiction of the Earth that corrected Ptolemy's geography.

Transmission. Robert of Chester (1145, Segovia) and Gerard of Cremona (Toledo, later 12th c.) translated the Algebra into Latin; it became Europe's introduction to the subject and was still cited by Italian algebraists in the 1500s. The arithmetic, through the algorismus literature, taught Europe decimal computation.

Sources: Rashed, The Development of Arabic Mathematics; Berggren, Episodes, ch. 4; Katz; DSB (G. Toomer, "al-Khwarizmi"). English translation of the Algebra: F. Rosen (1831), superseded by Rashed's edition (2009).

docs.title: al-Jawhari
docs.text:
al-Abbas ibn Said al-Jawhari (fl. c. 830) · Baghdad · geometry

A geometer of al-Ma'mun's circle who participated in the caliph's astronomical observations and wrote a commentary on Euclid's Elements, notable for containing one of the earliest recorded attempts in the Islamic world to prove Euclid's parallel postulate. The attempt fails (as all such attempts must), but it opens a research line, criticism of the parallel postulate, that runs through Thabit ibn Qurra, Ibn al-Haytham, Omar Khayyam, and Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, and which fed, via the 1594 Rome printing of a Tusi-attributed recension and its discussion by John Wallis and Girolamo Saccheri, into the prehistory of non-Euclidean geometry.

Sources: DSB; Rosenfeld, A History of Non-Euclidean Geometry.

docs.title: al-Kindi
docs.text:
Abu Yusuf Ya'qub ibn Ishaq al-Kindi (c. 801–873) · Baghdad · philosophy, mathematics, optics, cryptanalysis

"The Philosopher of the Arabs" wrote across an enormous range; his mathematical importance is threefold. First, his works on geometrical optics transmitted and corrected the Euclidean theory of vision and influenced Ibn al-Haytham. Second, his treatise On Deciphering Cryptographic Messages contains the earliest known description of frequency analysis, the statistical method for breaking substitution ciphers; this is the founding document of cryptanalysis and an early landmark of statistical reasoning, a point of direct relevance to modern cybersecurity curricula. Third, his numerous treatises on arithmetic helped popularize Indian numerals among the educated public.

Sources: Rashed (ed.), works on al-Kindi's optics; Ibrahim Al-Kadi, "Origins of Cryptology: The Arab Contributions," Cryptologia 16 (1992); Simon Singh, The Code Book (popular account).

docs.title: The Banu Musa
docs.text:
Muhammad, Ahmad, and al-Hasan, the "Sons of Musa" ibn Shakir (fl. c. 830–870, Muhammad d. 873) · Baghdad · geometry, mechanics

Three wealthy brothers who funded translations (they employed Thabit ibn Qurra, their greatest discovery) and did first-rate geometry of their own. Their Book on the Measurement of Plane and Spherical Figures treated areas and volumes in the manner of Archimedes but with a methodological novelty: they operated with the number \(\pi\) as a magnitude in its own right and presented Archimedean results in computational form. The book, translated by Gerard of Cremona as Verba filiorum, was a standard source for Archimedean geometry in Latin Europe and was used by Fibonacci and later by the 13th–14th century European geometers. Ahmad's Book of Ingenious Devices (automata, self-regulating mechanisms) belongs to the prehistory of control engineering.

Sources: Berggren, Episodes; DSB; Clagett, Archimedes in the Middle Ages, vol. 1.

docs.title: Habash al-Hasib
docs.text:
Ahmad ibn Abdallah Habash al-Hasib al-Marwazi ("Habash the Reckoner," fl. c. 825–870) · Baghdad, Samarra · astronomy, trigonometry

A working astronomer of al-Ma'mun's observational program whose zijes helped naturalize trigonometric methods. He is credited with early systematic use of the shadow functions, the quantities we now call tangent and cotangent, in tabulated form, and with auxiliary tables that simplified spherical-astronomical computation. Attributions of "first use" in this area are contested among historians (Abu al-Wafa and others consolidated the six standard functions later), but Habash's tables mark the point where trigonometry in the Islamic world begins to outgrow its Greek chord-based inheritance.

Sources: E. S. Kennedy, "A Survey of Islamic Astronomical Tables"; DSB.

docs.title: al-Mahani
docs.text:
Abu Abdallah Muhammad ibn Isa al-Mahani (fl. c. 860, d. c. 880) · Baghdad · geometry, algebra

Known for attempting to solve the Archimedean problem of dividing a sphere by a plane into segments with a given volume ratio (from On the Sphere and Cylinder II.4). Al-Mahani reduced it to a cubic equation, which he could not solve; the problem became famous in the tradition as "al-Mahani's equation" and was eventually handled by al-Khazin using conic sections. This episode began the research program, cubics via intersecting conics, that culminates in Omar Khayyam. He also wrote commentaries on Euclid Book X (irrational magnitudes), pushing the arithmetization of irrationals.

Sources: Berggren, Episodes; DSB; Rashed.

docs.title: Thabit ibn Qurra
docs.text:
Abu al-Hasan Thabit ibn Qurra al-Harrani (836–901) · Harran, then Baghdad · geometry, number theory, astronomy, mechanics

A Sabian from Harran recruited by the Banu Musa, Thabit became the finest geometer of the ninth century and one of the great mathematicians of the entire tradition.

Number theory. His theorem on amicable numbers gives a rule generating amicable pairs: if \(p = 3\cdot 2^{n-1} - 1\), \(q = 3\cdot 2^n - 1\), and \(r = 9\cdot 2^{2n-1} - 1\) are all prime for \(n > 1\), then \(2^n pq\) and \(2^n r\) are amicable. This is the first known general theorem producing amicable pairs; Fermat and Descartes rediscovered pairs derivable from it centuries later, and Euler generalized the rule.

Geometry and proto-calculus. He computed the area of a parabolic segment and volumes of paraboloids by summation methods that partition intervals into unequal parts, work squarely in the lineage from Archimedes' method of exhaustion toward integration. He wrote one of the serious early attempts on the parallel postulate and a generalization of the Pythagorean theorem to arbitrary triangles.

Translation and revision. He revised the Ishaq ibn Hunayn translations of Euclid and Ptolemy into the standard editions of the tradition, and translated or revised works of Archimedes and Apollonius, including Books V–VII of the Conics, which survive only in Arabic; without Thabit's school, a third of the Conics would be lost.

Transmission. His treatise on the qarastun (steelyard balance) circulated in Latin as Liber karastonis; his astronomical and geometric works influenced both the Islamic and, via translation, the Latin traditions.

Sources: Berggren, Episodes, chs. 2–3; Rashed; DSB (B. Rosenfeld and A. T. Grigorian, "Thabit ibn Qurra"); Roshdi Rashed (ed.), Thabit ibn Qurra: Science and Philosophy in Ninth-Century Baghdad (2009).

docs.title: Qusta ibn Luqa
docs.text:
Qusta ibn Luqa al-Ba'labakki (c. 820 – c. 912) · Baalbek, Baghdad, Armenia · translation, mathematics, medicine

A Greek Christian from Baalbek, fluent in Greek, who translated Diophantus's Arithmetica into Arabic (as "The Art of Algebra"), along with works of Theodosius, Autolycus, and Hero. The Arabic Diophantus is historically precious twice over: it shaped the number-theoretic algebra of al-Karaji and al-Samawal, and four of its books survive only in Qusta's Arabic version, discovered in manuscript in Mashhad and published in the 1970s–80s, doubling the extant Diophantus.

Sources: J. Sesiano, Books IV to VII of Diophantus' Arithmetica in the Arabic Translation (1982); Rashed's edition; DSB.

docs.title: al-Battani
docs.text:
Abu Abdallah Muhammad ibn Jabir al-Battani (c. 858–929) · Raqqa · astronomy, trigonometry

Latinized as Albategnius. Though his career extends past 900, he belongs with the foundational generation. His Kitab al-Zij (the Sabian Tables) rests on some forty years of his own observations at Raqqa and is the most influential single zij of the tradition in Europe. Mathematically, al-Battani used the sine systematically where Ptolemy had used chords, employed the relation equivalent to \(\tan\theta\) via shadow lengths, and stated the formula equivalent to the spherical law of cosines for his qibla-type problems. He determined the solar eccentricity and the obliquity of the ecliptic with accuracy that stood for centuries and discovered the motion of the solar apogee.

Transmission. Translated by Robert of Chester and, definitively, by Plato of Tivoli as De motu stellarum; printed in 1537. Copernicus cites al-Battani repeatedly in De revolutionibus, and his data was still used by Kepler and, for lunar acceleration studies, by Dunthorne in the eighteenth century.

Sources: DSB (W. Hartner, "al-Battani"); Kennedy, Survey; the standard edition is C. A. Nallino, Al-Battani sive Albatenii Opus Astronomicum (1899–1907).

docs.title: Era II — The Tenth Century (900–1000)
docs.text: The century of consolidation and specialization. Decimal fractions appear, the six trigonometric functions are completed, geometric construction becomes a refined art, and the tradition spreads west to Córdoba.

docs.title: Abu Kamil
docs.text:
Abu Kamil Shuja ibn Aslam (c. 850 – c. 930) · Egypt · algebra

"The Calculator from Egypt," the essential bridge between al-Khwarizmi and everything after. His Book on Algebra (Kitab fi al-jabr wa-l-muqabala) extends al-Khwarizmi decisively: he works comfortably with irrational coefficients and irrational solutions, manipulates surds with rules equivalent to \(\sqrt{a}\pm\sqrt{b} = \sqrt{a + b \pm 2\sqrt{ab}}\), handles powers of the unknown up to \(x^8\), and solves systems and indeterminate problems with real technical power. His treatise on the pentagon and decagon applies algebra to geometric construction problems, and his book on indeterminate problems overlaps the Diophantine tradition.

Transmission. Abu Kamil is a principal, documented source of Fibonacci's Liber Abaci (1202); many of Fibonacci's problems are Abu Kamil's, sometimes with the same numbers. A Latin translation and a Hebrew translation (by Mordecai Finzi, 15th c.) carried him into Europe independently.

Sources: Rashed's edition of Abu Kamil (2012); Berggren, Episodes; Katz; DSB.

docs.title: al-Nayrizi
docs.text:
Abu al-Abbas al-Fadl ibn Hatim al-Nayrizi (c. 865 – c. 922) · Baghdad · geometry, astronomy

Latinized as Anaritius. Author of the most important early Arabic commentary on Euclid's Elements, which preserves lost Greek material (including parts of Heron's and Simplicius's commentaries) and contains his own attempted proof of the parallel postulate. Gerard of Cremona translated the commentary into Latin, through which it influenced medieval European geometry teaching, including Albertus Magnus. He also wrote on the mathematics of the spherical astrolabe and on qibla determination.

Sources: DSB; Lo Bello's English editions of Anaritius; Rosenfeld.

docs.title: Sinan ibn Thabit and Ibrahim ibn Sinan
docs.text:
Sinan ibn Thabit (c. 880–943) and his son Ibrahim ibn Sinan (908–946) · Baghdad · geometry, astronomy

Thabit ibn Qurra's son Sinan was chiefly a physician and administrator of Baghdad's hospitals, but his son Ibrahim, dead at 38, was a geometer of the first rank. Ibrahim's quadrature of the parabola is simpler than Archimedes' own (a fact he advertised, family honor being at stake, since critics said his grandfather's proof was too long) and is arguably the most elegant pre-calculus parabola quadrature ever given, using an affine-invariance argument of striking modernity. His treatise On Analysis and Synthesis is one of the most sophisticated methodological works of the tradition, a study of mathematical discovery itself, and his work on drawing the conic sections gives practical pointwise constructions of ellipse, parabola, and hyperbola.

Sources: Berggren, Episodes; Rashed & Bellosta, Ibrahim ibn Sinan: Logique et géométrie au Xe siècle (2000); DSB.

docs.title: al-Uqlidisi
docs.text:
Abu al-Hasan Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Uqlidisi (fl. c. 952) · Damascus · arithmetic

His name means "the Euclidean," probably because he earned a living copying Euclid manuscripts. His Kitab al-Fusul fi al-Hisab al-Hindi ("Chapters on Hindu Reckoning," written 952/953 in Damascus) is the earliest surviving Arabic arithmetic on Indian numerals, and it contains the earliest known appearance of decimal fractions, complete with a notational mark (a stroke over the units digit) to mark the decimal place: he halves 19 five times to get 0.59375, written in pure decimal form. He also deliberately adapted the algorithms from the Indian dust board to pen and paper, an underappreciated step toward mathematics as a written, checkable discipline.

Historians long credited decimal fractions to al-Kashi (15th c.); A. S. Saidan's 1966 study and 1978 translation of al-Uqlidisi moved the date back nearly five centuries. Al-Kashi remains the one who made decimal fractions a systematic computational instrument.

Sources: A. S. Saidan, The Arithmetic of al-Uqlidisi (1978); Berggren, Episodes, ch. 2; Katz.

docs.title: al-Khazin
docs.text:
Abu Ja'far al-Khazin (d. c. 971) · Khurasan · algebra, geometry, astronomy

Solved "al-Mahani's equation," the cubic arising from Archimedes' sphere-division problem, by means of intersecting conic sections, the first known success of the method that Omar Khayyam would later systematize for all cubics. Also worked on number theory, including a treatment of the impossibility side of what we would call Fermat-type problems for certain cases (his proofs were incomplete), and on the isoperimetric problem.

Sources: Rashed; DSB; Berggren.

docs.title: Abu al-Wafa al-Buzjani
docs.text:
Abu al-Wafa Muhammad ibn Muhammad al-Buzjani (940–998) · Baghdad · trigonometry, geometry, arithmetic

One of the greatest of all the tradition's mathematicians, and the central figure in the completion of trigonometry.

Trigonometry. Abu al-Wafa worked with all six trigonometric functions (sine, cosine, tangent, cotangent, secant, cosecant), established the identities relating them, proved addition and double-angle theorems in a clean modern-style form (equivalent to \(\sin(a \pm b) = \sin a\cos b \pm \cos a\sin b\)), computed sine tables of unprecedented accuracy using a refined interpolation, and stated the spherical law of sines (priority contested with his contemporaries Abu Nasr Mansur and al-Khujandi; the three worked in overlapping circles and the sources do not settle it).

Practical geometry. His Book on What Is Necessary from Geometric Construction for the Artisan treats constructions with straightedge and a rusty compass (fixed opening), exact and approximate constructions of regular polygons, and the dissection problems behind the girih tile patterns of Islamic ornament. This work links high geometry to craft practice.

Arithmetic. His practical arithmetic for scribes and merchants includes the first recorded systematic treatment in Arabic of negative quantities as debts in a computational rule.

Transmission. His trigonometric consolidation flowed into every later zij and, through the Latin and Byzantine transmission of Islamic astronomy, into European trigonometry, where Regiomontanus's De triangulis (1464, printed 1533) organizes essentially the same material.

Sources: Berggren, Episodes, ch. 5; Katz; DSB (A. P. Youschkevitch, "Abu'l-Wafa"); Kennedy, Survey.

docs.title: al-Quhi
docs.text:
Abu Sahl Wayjan ibn Rustam al-Quhi (fl. c. 970–1000) · Tabaristan, Baghdad · geometry, astronomy

Regarded by contemporaries as the leading geometer of his day and director of the Buyid observatory in Baghdad (988). A virtuoso of Archimedean and Apollonian methods: he solved sphere-division and related problems via conics, studied the perfect compass (an instrument drawing any conic in one sweep), investigated centers of gravity, and pushed beyond Archimedes on problems of inscribing solids. His correspondence with Abu Ishaq al-Sabi is a rare surviving record of working mathematical discussion in the period.

Sources: Berggren's studies and editions of al-Quhi; Rashed, Geometry and Dioptrics; DSB.

docs.title: al-Sijzi
docs.text:
Abu Said Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Sijzi (c. 945 – c. 1020) · Sijistan, Shiraz · geometry

A specialist in the geometry of conic sections and geometric problem-solving; his treatise on the construction of the regular heptagon by conics is among the classics of the genre (the heptagon, impossible by straightedge and compass, was a proving ground for the tradition's conic-section methods). His methodological essay on making geometric problems tractable is an early "how to think about hard problems" text. He is also reported to have constructed an astrolabe based on the assumption of a rotating Earth, evidence such hypotheses were discussable.

Sources: Hogendijk's studies of al-Sijzi; Berggren; DSB.

docs.title: al-Khujandi
docs.text:
Abu Mahmud Hamid ibn al-Khidr al-Khujandi (c. 940–1000) · Rayy · astronomy, trigonometry

Builder of a giant sextant at Rayy (the largest observing instrument of its time) for measuring the obliquity of the ecliptic, an instance of the tradition's insight that instrument scale buys precision, later pushed further at Maragha and Samarkand. He is one of the claimants (with Abu al-Wafa and Abu Nasr Mansur) to the spherical law of sines, and he asserted (without a complete proof) the impossibility of integer solutions to \(x^3 + y^3 = z^3\), an early appearance of a Fermat's Last Theorem case in the literature.

Sources: DSB; Kennedy; Rashed.

docs.title: Ibn Sahl
docs.text:
Abu Sa'd al-Ala' ibn Sahl (fl. c. 984) · Baghdad · optics, geometry

Rescued from obscurity by Roshdi Rashed's 1990 reconstruction of his treatise On Burning Instruments: Ibn Sahl there analyzes refraction in lenses and states, geometrically, the constant-ratio relationship now called Snell's law, some six centuries before Snellius and Descartes. He used it to design plano-convex and biconvex burning lenses via the anaclastic problem. His work fed directly into Ibn al-Haytham's Optics. The finding rewrote the history of geometrical optics.

Sources: R. Rashed, "A Pioneer in Anaclastics: Ibn Sahl on Burning Mirrors and Lenses," Isis 81 (1990); Rashed, Geometry and Dioptrics in Classical Islam.

docs.title: al-Saghani
docs.text:
Abu Hamid al-Saghani (d. 990) · Baghdad · astronomy, geometry

Astronomer at the Buyid observatory and instrument maker (his name is associated with fine astrolabes). Mathematically he is remembered for work on the trisection of the angle, one of the three classical Greek problems, by neusis-type and conic methods, part of the tradition's systematic treatment of problems beyond straightedge and compass.

Sources: DSB; Berggren.

docs.title: Maslama al-Majriti
docs.text:
Maslama ibn Ahmad al-Majriti (c. 950–1007) · Córdoba · astronomy, mathematics

The scholar who naturalized eastern mathematical astronomy in al-Andalus. He adapted al-Khwarizmi's zij to the meridian of Córdoba and the Hijra calendar (this adaptation, in Adelard of Bath's Latin translation, is the version that survives, the original being lost), edited Ptolemy's Planisphaerium (again surviving through the Arabic-Latin line), and founded the school from which Andalusi mathematics and astronomy descend: his students' students include the makers of the Toledan Tables. Through Córdoba, the mathematics of Baghdad began its westward journey toward Latin Europe.

Sources: DSB; Samsó, Las ciencias de los antiguos en al-Andalus; Kennedy, Survey.

docs.title: Ibn Yunus
docs.text:
Abu al-Hasan Ali ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Yunus (c. 950–1009) · Cairo · astronomy, trigonometry

Court astronomer to the Fatimid caliphs; his enormous Hakimi Zij rests on decades of observations from Cairo, many still usable by modern astronomers studying the secular acceleration of the Moon (Simon Newcomb used his eclipse records in the 19th century). Mathematically, his tables display extraordinary computational technique, and he is associated with a prosthaphaeresis-type identity, equivalent to \(\cos a\cos b = \frac{1}{2}[\cos(a-b)+\cos(a+b)]\), of the kind that sixteenth-century European astronomers later used to convert multiplication into addition, the immediate precursor idea to logarithms. (Direct influence of Ibn Yunus on the European prosthaphaeresis school is not documented; the parallel is conceptual.)

Sources: DSB (D. King, "Ibn Yunus"); King, "Islamic Astronomy," in Walker (ed.), Astronomy before the Telescope; Kennedy, Survey.

docs.title: al-Karaji
docs.text:
Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Karaji (c. 953 – c. 1029) · Baghdad · algebra, arithmetic, engineering

(Sometimes written al-Karkhi in older literature.) The pivotal figure in the arithmetization of algebra: where al-Khwarizmi justified algebra geometrically, al-Karaji cut it loose. In al-Fakhri, al-Badi, and al-Kafi fi al-hisab, he treats the arithmetic of polynomial expressions systematically, powers \(x, x^2, x^3, \dots\) and their reciprocals as an indexed sequence, with rules for operating on polynomials as such, effectively founding polynomial algebra. He gave the table of binomial coefficients with the additive generation rule (the "Pascal's triangle" recurrence \(\binom{n}{k} = \binom{n-1}{k-1} + \binom{n-1}{k}\)), known from al-Samawal's report of his lost work, and used an early form of argument by recursion/induction in proving results like the sum-of-cubes formula \(\left(\sum k\right)^2 = \sum k^3\).

His practical side: The Extraction of Hidden Waters, a serious engineering treatise on groundwater and qanat construction, containing applied geometry and surveying.

Transmission. The al-Karaji school (through al-Samawal) parallels and anticipates the algebraic techniques of the European Renaissance; direct textual transmission to Europe is limited, making this a case study in independent re-development along a path the Islamic tradition had already walked.

Sources: Rashed, The Development of Arabic Mathematics: Between Arithmetic and Algebra; Katz; DSB; Woepcke's 1853 study of al-Fakhri (historic first Western notice).

docs.title: Kushyar ibn Labban
docs.text:
Kushyar ibn Labban al-Jili (c. 971–1029) · Gilan, Baghdad region · arithmetic, astronomy

Author of Principles of Hindu Reckoning (Usul Hisab al-Hind), one of the clearest surviving textbooks of decimal arithmetic, translated into English by Levey and Petruck (1965). It teaches the full algorithm suite including square and cube root extraction, and shows sexagesimal (base-60) computation as used by astronomers alongside decimal, exactly the dual-base fluency the profession required. His zijes were widely used, and his student al-Nasawi continued the arithmetic textbook tradition.

Sources: Levey & Petruck, Kushyar ibn Labban: Principles of Hindu Reckoning (1965); DSB; Kennedy.

docs.title: Era III — The Golden Age (c. 1000–1100)
docs.text: The eleventh century produced several of the greatest scientists of the entire medieval world, East or West: Ibn al-Haytham, al-Biruni, and (spilling into the twelfth century) Omar Khayyam. Meanwhile al-Andalus matured into a mathematical center whose output would soon flow into Latin.

docs.title: Abu Nasr Mansur
docs.text:
Abu Nasr Mansur ibn Ali ibn Iraq (c. 960 – c. 1036) · Khwarazm, Ghazna · trigonometry, geometry

A prince of the Khwarazmian ruling house, teacher and lifelong collaborator of al-Biruni (they exchanged dedicated treatises for decades). One of the three claimants to the spherical law of sines, and author of the definitive Arabic edition of Menelaus's Spherics, the foundation text of spherical geometry, which survives through his recension. His work systematically replaced the cumbersome Menelaus configuration theorem with the cleaner sine-rule methods that made spherical astronomy computationally humane.

Sources: DSB; Berggren, Episodes, ch. 6; Kennedy.

docs.title: al-Nasawi
docs.text:
Abu al-Hasan Ali ibn Ahmad al-Nasawi (c. 1011 – c. 1075) · Khurasan, Baghdad · arithmetic

Student of Kushyar ibn Labban's tradition; his al-Muqni fi al-Hisab al-Hindi (written first in Persian, then Arabic) continued the decimal-arithmetic textbook line, treating fractions, root extraction (with the approximation refinements typical of the school), and criticizing his predecessors' expositions. Useful to historians precisely because he reviews and compares earlier methods.

Sources: DSB; Saidan's studies of Arabic arithmetic.

docs.title: Ibn Tahir al-Baghdadi
docs.text:
Abd al-Qahir ibn Tahir al-Baghdadi (d. 1037) · Baghdad, Nishapur · arithmetic, number theory

Theologian and mathematician; his al-Takmila fi al-Hisab ("Completion of Arithmetic") surveys the number systems in concurrent use, Indian decimal, finger-reckoning, sexagesimal, and treats topics in number theory including a result on equivalent numbers (pairs with equal sums of proper divisors of some value) beyond the Greek material, and an improved discussion of amicable and perfect numbers.

Sources: Saidan's edition and studies; DSB.

docs.title: Ibn al-Haytham
docs.text:
Abu Ali al-Hasan ibn al-Haytham (c. 965 – c. 1040) · Basra, then Cairo · optics, geometry, astronomy, method

Latinized as Alhazen (from al-Hasan). One of the most important scientists of the Middle Ages in any civilization.

Optics. The seven-book Kitab al-Manazir ("Book of Optics," c. 1011–1021, composed in Cairo) refounded the science of vision on the intromission theory (light travels from objects to the eye), fused the mathematical (Euclid, Ptolemy) and medical (Galen) traditions, and, decisively for the history of science, argued by systematic experiment: controlled setups with dark chambers (the camera obscura analyzed properly for the first time), apertures, and measured refractions. "Alhazen's problem", find the reflection point on a spherical mirror between given object and eye, reduces to a quartic he solved geometrically via conics; algebraic solutions were only achieved by European mathematicians centuries later (Huygens gave a famous treatment).

Mathematics. He summed the fourth powers \(\sum k^4\) (and gave a method extending to any integer power) using a telescoping/recursive argument, and used the result to compute the volume of a paraboloid of revolution about its base, a genuine integration in all but name; the summation formulas are exactly the ones Cavalieri and Fermat needed for \(\int x^n\,dx\) in the seventeenth century. He attempted the parallel postulate via what is now called the "Lambert quadrilateral" configuration (three right angles, investigate the fourth), studied lunes and the quadrature of circle-related figures, and wrote On the Analysis and Synthesis of Mathematical Problems.

Astronomy. His Doubts Concerning Ptolemy (al-Shukuk ala Batlamyus) catalogued the physical inconsistencies of Ptolemaic planetary models (equant, prosneusis), setting the critical agenda that the Maragha school later executed.

Transmission. The Optics was translated into Latin around 1200 as De aspectibus / Perspectiva and shaped everyone: Roger Bacon, Witelo, Pecham, the Renaissance perspectivists (Ghiberti cited him), and Kepler, whose Ad Vitellionem Paralipomena (1604), the founding work of modern optics, is framed as a supplement to the Alhazen-Witelo tradition. Risner's 1572 printed edition Opticae thesaurus was standard into the seventeenth century.

Sources: A. I. Sabra's edition and English translation of the Optics, Books I–III (1989); Sabra's DSB article "Ibn al-Haytham"; Rashed, Les mathématiques infinitésimales du IXe au XIe siècle; Katz; A. Mark Smith, From Sight to Light (2015).

docs.title: al-Biruni
docs.text:
Abu Rayhan Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-Biruni (973–1048) · Khwarazm, Ghazna · mathematics, astronomy, geodesy, history of science

Perhaps the most universal scholar of the era: mathematician, astronomer, geographer, historian, linguist (he learned Sanskrit and wrote the great ethnographic-scientific study India), and mineralogist. Mathematical highlights:

Geodesy. His measurement of the Earth's radius by observing the dip of the horizon from a mountain of measured height (in the Punjab region) is a famous set piece of applied trigonometry, requiring only an astrolabe and the mountain, and yielding a value close to modern figures (manuscript unit uncertainties make exact accuracy claims slippery; the method is the point).

Trigonometry. His Qanun al-Mas'udi (the "Mas'udic Canon," c. 1030s), an astronomical encyclopedia, contains state-of-the-art trigonometric tables and methods; his separate treatise on chords collects and proves a wealth of circle geometry. He treated the qibla problem definitively in The Determination of the Coordinates of Cities, a monograph of mathematical geography.

Numerical analysis. To trisect angles / compute \(\sin 1°\) (which leads to an irreducible cubic), he used iterative and interpolation techniques of high sophistication, and he explicitly discussed the cubic equation for the regular nonagon's chord.

The shadow. His Exhaustive Treatise on Shadows is the fullest medieval study of the tangent and cotangent functions and gnomonics.

Transmission. Little of al-Biruni was translated into Latin, making him the standing example that the Islamic tradition's ceiling was far above what Europe received. His work was hugely influential eastward (Persia, India) and is now a primary source for historians of multiple civilizations.

Sources: E. S. Kennedy's numerous al-Biruni studies; DSB (Kennedy, "al-Biruni"); Berggren, Episodes, ch. 6; English translations: Sachau (India, Chronology), Jamil Ali (Coordinates of Cities), Kennedy (Shadows).

docs.title: Ibn Sina
docs.text:
Abu Ali al-Husayn ibn Sina (980–1037) · Bukhara, Persia · philosophy, medicine, with mathematical sections

Latinized as Avicenna. Included here for completeness: his encyclopedic Kitab al-Shifa ("Book of Healing") contains substantial mathematical sections, a recension of Euclid, an arithmetic treating topics like the casting-out-of-nines check with a proof-oriented attitude, music theory, and astronomy, which shaped how mathematics was taught within philosophy curricula for centuries in both the Islamic world and (via Latin translation of parts of the Shifa) Europe. Not an original mathematician of the first rank, but a major channel of mathematical culture.

Sources: DSB; Katz.

docs.title: Ibn al-Samh and the school of al-Andalus
docs.text:
Ibn al-Samh (984–1035, Granada) · geometry, astronomy · and al-Zarqali (Azarquiel) (c. 1029–1100, Toledo/Córdoba) · astronomy, instruments

Ibn al-Samh, a student of Maslama al-Majriti's school, wrote on the cylinder's sections (his treatise on the ellipse as a plane section survives through Hebrew transmission) and on the astrolabe. Al-Zarqali, a generation later, is the towering Andalusi figure: principal author of the Toledan Tables, the zij (adapted from al-Khwarizmi, al-Battani, and new Toledo observations) that, in Latin translation, became the standard astronomical tables of Europe for two centuries, until superseded by the Alfonsine Tables (which were themselves produced by a Castilian court program working in the Arabic tradition). He invented the safiha (saphaea), a universal astrolabe plate usable at any latitude, described Mercury's orbit with an oval curve, and his value for the motion of the solar apogee was cited by Copernicus in De revolutionibus.

Sources: DSB (J. Vernet, "al-Zarqali"); Samsó; Kennedy, Survey; Toomer's study of the Toledan Tables.

docs.title: Ibn Muadh al-Jayyani
docs.text:
Abu Abdallah Muhammad ibn Muadh al-Jayyani (989 – c. 1079) · Jaén, al-Andalus · trigonometry, astronomy

Author of The Book of Unknown Arcs of a Sphere, the first treatise devoted to spherical trigonometry as an independent subject (rather than a chapter of astronomy), systematically solving spherical triangles from given parts. Whether he drew on the eastern school (Abu Nasr et al.) or worked independently is debated; either way the treatise marks trigonometry's arrival in al-Andalus as a mature discipline, conveniently placed for transmission northward. His treatise on twilight (estimating atmospheric refraction height) circulated in Latin, long misattributed to Alhazen.

Sources: M. V. Villuendas's edition; DSB; Van Brummelen, The Mathematics of the Heavens and the Earth.

docs.title: al-Mu'taman ibn Hud
docs.text:
Yusuf al-Mu'taman ibn Hud (d. 1085) · Zaragoza · geometry

King of the taifa of Zaragoza (r. 1081–1085) and a serious research geometer, a combination with few parallels. His Kitab al-Istikmal ("Book of Perfection"), rediscovered and analyzed by Jan Hogendijk in the 1980s, is a synthesis of the Greek and Arabic geometric corpus containing original results, including the theorem on the ratios cut on a triangle's cevians now known as Ceva's theorem, six centuries before Giovanni Ceva (1678). No transmission route from Zaragoza to Ceva is documented; it stands as an independent anticipation. The Istikmal circulated east (Maimonides knew and taught it).

Sources: J. P. Hogendijk, "Discovery of an 11th-century geometrical compilation: the Istikmal of Yusuf al-Mu'taman ibn Hud," Historia Mathematica 13 (1986); DSB supplement.

docs.title: Omar Khayyam
docs.text:
Ghiyath al-Din Abu al-Fath Umar ibn Ibrahim al-Khayyami (1048–1131) · Nishapur, Isfahan · algebra, geometry, astronomy (and, by attribution, poetry)

In the West famous for the Rubaiyat (the attribution of much of that poetry is a separate scholarly tangle); in the history of mathematics, famous for two achievements.

The cubics. His Treatise on Demonstration of Problems of Algebra (c. 1070, Isfahan) gives the first systematic theory of cubic equations: he classifies all cubics (fourteen types not reducible to lower degree, under positive-coefficient conventions), and solves every type geometrically by intersecting conic sections, a circle with a parabola, two hyperbolas, and so on, proving the constructions correct. He states frankly that he could not find arithmetical (algebraic) solutions and expresses hope that successors would, a hope fulfilled in 1520s–1540s Italy (del Ferro, Tartaglia, Cardano). He also recognized that cubics can have two (positive) roots, and his remark that "algebra is not a collection of tricks but geometric facts proved" captures the discipline's new self-understanding. Whether Italian algebraists knew Khayyam's text is doubtful (no Latin translation is known); the geometric-conics approach, however, reappears in Descartes' Géométrie (1637), which solves cubics and quartics by intersecting conics in exactly Khayyam's spirit.

The parallels and ratios. His Explanation of the Difficulties in the Postulates of Euclid (1077) attacks the parallel postulate via the birectangular quadrilateral (equal sides perpendicular to the base; decide whether the summit angles are right, acute, or obtuse), the exact figure later called the Saccheri quadrilateral (1733), and refutes the acute/obtuse cases only by importing an equivalent postulate, as all such attempts must. The same work deepens the theory of ratio and proportion, arguing for treating ratios as numbers, a step toward the modern real-number concept.

The calendar. As head of the Isfahan observatory under Malik-Shah, he led the reform producing the Jalali calendar (1079), whose intercalation scheme yields a mean year accurate to roughly a day in several thousand years, more accurate than the Gregorian rule.

Sources: Rashed & Vahabzadeh, Omar Khayyam the Mathematician (2000); Berggren, Episodes, ch. 4; Katz; DSB (Youschkevitch & Rosenfeld, "al-Khayyami"); Rosenfeld, A History of Non-Euclidean Geometry.

docs.title: Era IV — The Twelfth Century (1100–1200)
docs.text: The century in which Europe began translating this tradition into Latin (see The Translation Movement) while the tradition itself pressed on: symbolic-style polynomial arithmetic, an astonishing proto-analytic treatment of cubics, and the flowering of Maghrebi calculation.

docs.title: al-Khazini
docs.text:
Abd al-Rahman al-Khazini (fl. c. 1115–1130) · Merv · mechanics, astronomy

A former slave of Byzantine origin who became a leading scientist at the Seljuk court in Merv. His Book of the Balance of Wisdom (Kitab Mizan al-Hikma, 1121/22) is the most comprehensive medieval treatise on mathematical statics and hydrostatics: theory of centers of gravity (building on al-Quhi and Ibn al-Haytham), the hydrostatic balance, and tables of specific gravities of metals, gems, and liquids measured to impressive precision. It treats gravity as directed toward the center of the Earth and varying with distance in a qualitative sense, mechanics as a mathematical science, four centuries before Stevin and Galilei retraced parts of this ground. His Sanjari Zij served practical astronomy.

Sources: DSB (R. E. Hall, "al-Khazini"); partial English translation by N. Khanikoff (1859).

docs.title: Jabir ibn Aflah
docs.text:
Abu Muhammad Jabir ibn Aflah (fl. c. 1120–1150) · Seville · astronomy, trigonometry

Latinized as Geber (a persistent source of confusion with the alchemist Jabir ibn Hayyan). His Islah al-Majisti ("Correction of the Almagest") criticized Ptolemy, notably re-ordering Venus and Mercury above the Sun, and, importantly for mathematics, opened with a self-contained treatise on spherical trigonometry organized around the sine rule and the rule of four quantities, discarding the Menelaus theorem entirely. Gerard of Cremona translated it into Latin; through this channel Jabir's trigonometry reached Regiomontanus, whose De triangulis omnibus borrows results from Geber (Cardano later pointedly accused Regiomontanus of insufficient acknowledgment). "Geber's theorem" in spherical trigonometry (\(\cos B = \cos b \sin A\) for a right spherical triangle, in one common statement) carries his Latin name to this day.

Sources: DSB (R. Lorch, "Jabir ibn Aflah"); Lorch's studies of the Islah; Van Brummelen.

docs.title: al-Samawal
docs.text:
al-Samawal ibn Yahya al-Maghribi (c. 1130 – c. 1180) · Baghdad, Persia · algebra, arithmetic

Born to a Jewish family in Baghdad (he converted to Islam in adulthood and wrote about it), a prodigy who composed his masterpiece al-Bahir fi al-Jabr ("The Dazzling in Algebra") around age nineteen, consolidating and extending the al-Karaji school.

Polynomial arithmetic. Al-Samawal manipulates polynomials via tables of coefficients indexed by power, including negative powers, performing addition, multiplication, and crucially long division of polynomials exactly as taught today, and carrying quotients into infinitely continuing expansions (e.g., dividing to obtain what is in effect a power series in \(1/x\)), with an explicit statement of the rule \(x^m \cdot x^n = x^{m+n}\) spanning negative exponents: "operating on unknowns with all the arithmetical tools the arithmetician applies to the known." Historians (Rashed) treat this as the clearest medieval statement of the program of arithmetizing algebra.

Induction-style proof. His proofs of the binomial coefficient recurrence and of identities like the sum of squares proceed by regression from \(n\) to \(n-1\) down to a base case, the recognizable skeleton of mathematical induction before its formalization (Pascal, 1654).

Approximation. In al-Qiwami he computes with decimal fractions and approximates roots by methods equivalent to keeping arbitrarily many decimal places, aware of controlled precision.

Sources: Rashed & Ahmad's edition of al-Bahir (1972); Rashed, Development of Arabic Mathematics; Katz; DSB.

docs.title: Sharaf al-Din al-Tusi
docs.text:
Sharaf al-Din al-Muzaffar ibn Muhammad al-Tusi (c. 1135 – c. 1213) · Tus, Damascus, Aleppo, Mosul · algebra, geometry

(Not to be confused with Nasir al-Din al-Tusi of the next century.) His Treatise on Equations takes Khayyam's classification of cubics and asks the next question: when do solutions exist, and how many? For cubic types that can lack positive solutions, he determines the condition by locating the maximum of the cubic expression: for \(x^3 + c = bx\) (his style, rendered in modern notation), he identifies the critical value \(x = \sqrt{b/3}\), where the expression \(bx - x^3\) is greatest, and compares \(c\) with that maximum to count roots. The critical value is precisely the root of what we would call the derivative, and the historian Roshdi Rashed has argued this amounts to a local-maximum analysis anticipating differential ideas; other historians (Hogendijk, Berggren) offer more conservative readings via Euclidean tools. Either way, the treatise also contains a remarkable numerical method for approximating cubic roots digit by digit (related to what is now called the Ruffini–Horner scheme, independently central in Chinese mathematics and formalized in Europe in 1804–1819). He also invented the linear astrolabe ("al-Tusi's staff"), a rod-form astrolabe.

Sources: Rashed's edition, Sharaf al-Din al-Tusi: Oeuvres mathématiques (1986); J. P. Hogendijk, "Sharaf al-Din al-Tusi on the number of positive roots of cubic equations," Historia Mathematica 16 (1989); Berggren's review discussions; DSB.

docs.title: al-Hassar
docs.text:
Abu Bakr Muhammad al-Hassar (fl. 12th century) · Maghreb (Ceuta or Fez region) · arithmetic

Author of Kitab al-Bayan wa-l-Tadhkar, a practical arithmetic of the Maghrebi school whose lasting monument is notational: al-Hassar's text contains the earliest known systematic use of the horizontal fraction bar, writing a fraction as numerator over denominator separated by a bar, the notation the entire world now uses. Fibonacci, educated partly in Bugia (in the Maghreb), uses precisely this notation in the Liber Abaci, the plausible route into Europe. The treatise was translated into Hebrew (by Moses ibn Tibbon, 1271), evidence of its circulation.

Sources: Lamrabet, Introduction à l'histoire des mathématiques maghrébines; Djebbar's studies of Maghrebi mathematics; Katz.

docs.title: Ibn al-Yasamin
docs.text:
Abu Muhammad Abdallah ibn al-Yasamin (d. c. 1204) · Maghreb, Marrakesh, Seville · arithmetic, algebra, pedagogy

A Berber scholar famous for mathematical didactic poems, above all the Urjuza fi al-jabr ("Poem on Algebra"), which versified the rules of algebra so students could memorize them; it was recited, memorized, and commented on across North Africa for centuries, a reminder that this tradition invested seriously in pedagogy. His school's manuscripts also display the developing Maghrebi algebraic symbolism (letters/marks for the unknown, its powers, roots, and equality) that al-Qalasadi would later systematize.

Sources: Djebbar; Abdeljaouad's studies of Maghrebi symbolism; Lamrabet.

docs.title: Era V — Maragha and the Thirteenth Century (1200–1300)
docs.text: After the Mongol conquest of Baghdad (1258), the scientific center of gravity moved to the great observatory at Maragha in northwestern Persia, founded 1259 under Hulagu Khan at the urging of Nasir al-Din al-Tusi. Maragha functioned as a research institute with a library, instrument workshops, international staff (including at least one Chinese astronomer), and a research program: repairing the physical inconsistencies of Ptolemaic astronomy with new mathematical devices. In the west, the Maghrebi school perfected the arithmetic textbook.

docs.title: Nasir al-Din al-Tusi
docs.text:
Muhammad ibn Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Tusi (1201–1274) · Tus, Alamut, Maragha · trigonometry, astronomy, geometry, philosophy

The dominant scientific personality of the century: philosopher, theologian, astronomer, mathematician, and scientific administrator who persuaded a Mongol conqueror to fund an observatory.

Trigonometry as an independent science. His Kitab al-Shakl al-qatta ("Treatise on the Complete Quadrilateral," c. 1260) is the first comprehensive treatise in which trigonometry is developed for its own sake, detached from astronomy: systematic plane and spherical trigonometry, the six functions, the plane and spherical laws of sines with proofs, and the complete solution of triangles from given data, including the polar-triangle method for the case of three given angles on the sphere. Nothing comparable exists in Europe until Regiomontanus's De triangulis (written 1464), which covers much the same ground; whether Regiomontanus had indirect access to Tusi-school material remains debated among historians.

The Tusi couple. In his Tadhkira fi ilm al-hay'a ("Memoir on Astronomy," 1261), Tusi introduced the theorem that if one circle rolls inside another of twice the diameter, any point on the small circle traces a straight line, the "Tusi couple." It converts two uniform circular motions into linear oscillation, letting astronomers eliminate Ptolemy's equant and build planetary models from uniform circular motions only. Mathematically it is a special case of hypocycloid motion; mechanically it reappears in engineering as a straight-line linkage principle. The same geometric device, with the same diagram lettering in a key manuscript comparison, appears in Copernicus's De revolutionibus (1543), III.4; whether Copernicus reinvented it or received it via Byzantine Greek intermediaries (a Greek manuscript of Tusi-couple material reached Italy in the 15th century) is one of the liveliest debates in the history of astronomy. See Renaissance Connections.

Geometry and the parallels. His recension of Euclid and his discussion of the parallel postulate continued the Khayyam line; a related work published in Rome in 1594 under his name (now usually attributed to his son or school, "pseudo-Tusi") was read by John Wallis and cited by Saccheri in Euclides ab omni naevo vindicatus (1733), placing the Islamic parallels tradition documentably in the direct prehistory of non-Euclidean geometry.

Editions. His tahrir (recensions) of Euclid, Ptolemy, and the "middle books" (Archimedes, Apollonius, Menelaus, Theodosius, Autolycus, Thabit et al.) became the standard curriculum of Islamic mathematics for centuries, a one-man textbook publishing program.

Sources: DSB (S. H. Nasr, "al-Tusi"); F. J. Ragep, Nasir al-Din al-Tusi's Memoir on Astronomy (1993, edition and translation of the Tadhkira); Van Brummelen; Rosenfeld; Saliba, Islamic Science and the Making of the European Renaissance.

docs.title: al-Urdi
docs.text:
Mu'ayyad al-Din al-Urdi (d. 1266) · Damascus, then Maragha · astronomy, geometry, engineering

Chief instrument builder of the Maragha observatory (his treatise describing its instruments survives) and author of Kitab al-Hay'a, which introduced Urdi's lemma: an equant-eliminating geometric transformation (an epicyclet device converting non-uniform motion about one center into uniform motion about another) developed before the observatory's founding. Urdi's lemma plus the Tusi couple form the standard toolkit of the Maragha planetary program, and the lemma reappears, again exactly, in Copernicus's models for the superior planets; Copernicus does not prove it, which historians (Saliba, Swerdlow) read as suggestive of inheritance rather than reinvention. That inference remains debated.

Sources: G. Saliba's edition and studies of al-Urdi; Swerdlow & Neugebauer, Mathematical Astronomy in Copernicus's De Revolutionibus; DSB.

docs.title: Muhyi al-Din al-Maghribi
docs.text:
Muhyi al-Din al-Maghribi (c. 1220–1283) · al-Andalus/Maghreb, Damascus, Maragha · trigonometry, astronomy

A westerner who joined the Maragha staff after the fall of Damascus. He conducted a long observational program at Maragha (his records, analyzed by George Saliba, are among the best evidence of the observatory's actual working methods) and computed new planetary parameters. Mathematically, he worked on the classical problems (angle trisection, the regular heptagon), on Euclid's parallel postulate, and on precision computation of chords and sines, including an iterative determination of the chord of 1°, a line al-Kashi would perfect.

Sources: Saliba's studies of al-Maghribi's observations; DSB; Rosenfeld & Ihsanoglu's bio-bibliography.

docs.title: Qutb al-Din al-Shirazi
docs.text:
Qutb al-Din Mahmud al-Shirazi (1236–1311) · Shiraz, Maragha, Tabriz · astronomy, optics, medicine

Student of Nasir al-Din al-Tusi at Maragha; polymath (he also produced a famous commentary on Avicenna's medical Canon). In astronomy his Nihayat al-Idrak and al-Tuhfa al-Shahiyya refined non-Ptolemaic planetary modeling, work continued by his student al-Farisi in optics and paralleled later by Ibn al-Shatir. In optics, he encouraged al-Farisi's re-examination of Ibn al-Haytham, which produced the first correct qualitative explanation of the rainbow (see al-Farisi, Era VI); Shirazi himself sketched the double-refraction-plus-reflection idea. The Shirazi–Farisi rainbow work is contemporary with, and independent of, Theodoric of Freiberg's similar European account (c. 1304–1310), a striking case of simultaneous discovery from the shared Alhazen inheritance.

Sources: DSB; Boyer, The Rainbow: From Myth to Mathematics; Saliba.

docs.title: Ibn al-Banna
docs.text:
Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn al-Banna al-Marrakushi (1256 – c. 1321) · Marrakesh, Fez · arithmetic, algebra, combinatorics

The great systematizer of the Maghrebi school. His Talkhis amal al-hisab ("Summary of Arithmetical Operations") became the arithmetic textbook of North Africa for two centuries, generating dozens of commentaries (including al-Qalasadi's, the vehicle for symbolic notation). It covers decimal arithmetic, fractions with the bar notation, proportion, root approximation (including the refinement \(\sqrt{a^2+r} \approx a + \frac{r}{2a+1}\)-type rules), false position, and algebra.

Combinatorics. In Raf al-Hijab, Ibn al-Banna derives rules equivalent to the formulas for combinations and permutations, \(\binom{n}{k}\) via the multiplicative rule \(\binom{n}{k}=\frac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)}{k!}\), motivated partly by a genuinely combinatorial tradition in Maghrebi scholarship (counting words, astrological conjunctions, and the like) that runs back through Ibn Munim's Fiqh al-Hisab (early 13th c., Marrakesh), where Pascal's-triangle tables are built for counting problems, one of the earliest places anywhere that the binomial table is read combinatorially rather than algebraically.

Sources: Djebbar's editions and studies; A. Djebbar & M. Aballagh on Ibn al-Banna; Katz (which discusses Ibn Munim's combinatorics); Lamrabet.

docs.title: Era VI — The Fourteenth Century (1300–1400)
docs.text: Damascus becomes a center of astronomical computation of staggering ambition; number theory and optics reach new peaks in Persia; the Maghrebi textbook tradition rolls on.

docs.title: Kamal al-Din al-Farisi
docs.text:
Kamal al-Din al-Farisi (c. 1267–1319) · Tabriz · optics, number theory

Student of Qutb al-Din al-Shirazi and the deepest mathematical mind of his generation in two separate fields.

Optics.
